title: Season early and in layers, not just at the end
claim: Salting early and at each stage seasons food all the way through; salt added only at the end sits on the surface and hits the tongue as a harsh, uneven coating.
action: Salt at the start so it has time to penetrate, then taste and adjust as you build, rather than dumping it all in at the finish.

variants.note: Salt the meat directly under the skin; the skin blocks surface salt from reaching the flesh.
Dissolve the salt in a little liquid and toss, so it slips under the shells where you can't salt directly.

mechanism: Salt migrates into food slowly, faster with heat but never instantly; applied early it seasons throughout, applied late it only coats the surface.
render_hint: Name the actual ingredient and the stage in this recipe where seasoning happens; pick the variant only if it matches.
source_note: interpreted from general salting technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #1

title: Bloom spices in fat or they taste raw
claim: Stirring ground spices or a paste into hot fat before any liquid unlocks their full flavor; skip it and the spice character stays shallow and powdery.
action: Cook the spices in the fat until fragrant before adding liquid, watching the clock so they don't scorch.
signal: No aroma when the spices hit the fat means too cool; smoke or fast-darkening specks mean about to burn.
failure_mode: Flat, raw, powdery spice flavor (under-bloomed) or an acrid, scorched note (over-bloomed).

variants.note: Stir into the fat with the aromatics; fragrant in 1-2 min.
Into shimmering fat, cook longer; ready when fragrant and visibly darkened.

mechanism: Many spice flavor compounds are fat-soluble; warming them in oil disperses them through the dish.
render_hint: Name the actual spices and fat, and pick the dry-blend or paste variant to match.
source_note: interpreted from general spice-blooming technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #2

title: A finishing drizzle or sprinkle wakes a dish up
claim: A last-second hit of acid, good oil, fresh herbs, or flaky salt adds brightness, aroma, and crunch that cooking flattens.
action: Hold back a finisher and add it to the plated dish, then taste once more before serving.

variants.note: Use a coarse or flaky salt so it keeps its crunch instead of dissolving into the dish.
Drizzle a flavored oil or a squeeze of acid over the finished dish for richness and lift.
A lone spice (sumac, Aleppo, celery salt) finishes as well as a blend; sprinkle evenly right before serving.

mechanism: Cooking dulls volatile aromas and softens texture; a raw finish restores contrast in flavor, aroma, and crunch.
render_hint: Suggest a finisher that fits this recipe's cuisine and ingredients; don't invent one that clashes.
source_note: interpreted from general finishing technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #3

title: Add the oil slowly or the vinaigrette breaks
claim: An emulsion forms only when oil is broken into fine droplets and dispersed into the acid; add it all at once and oil and acid stay separate.
action: Add the oil in stages while whisking hard, or shake in a sealed jar; a little mustard helps it come together and hold.
signal: Oil pooling on top instead of thickening into a uniform, slightly cloudy mixture.
failure_mode: Dressing splits into an oily layer over a watery one and tastes sharply acidic in spots.

variants.note: Whisk or shake with a bit of mustard; it holds long enough to dress the salad.
Include an emulsifier such as mustard so it survives sitting without separating.

mechanism: Vigorous mixing disperses oil into droplets small enough to stay suspended in the acid; an emulsifier coats them so they don't recombine.
render_hint: Name the actual acid and oil in this recipe; choose the make-ahead variant only if it's batched.
source_note: interpreted from general vinaigrette/emulsion technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #4

title: Acidic marinades turn proteins mushy if left too long
claim: Marinades flavor mainly the surface and salt does the deeper work; too long in acid denatures the exterior into a chalky or mushy layer, worst on fish and seafood.
action: Keep acidic marinades short (seafood minutes, poultry and meat a few hours) and rely on salt and aromatics for flavor that goes deeper.
signal: The surface looking opaque or 'cooked' and feeling soft before it ever hits heat.
failure_mode: Mushy, chalky exterior with an unpleasant texture after cooking.
mechanism: Acid denatures surface proteins over time the way heat does; salt diffuses inward to season, but acid mostly degrades texture at the surface.
render_hint: Match the time guidance to the specific protein in this recipe.
source_note: interpreted from general marinating technique

title: Pour hot brine over vegetables for fast pickles
claim: A hot vinegar-sugar-salt brine poured over raw vegetables penetrates fast, giving bright, crisp pickles in under an hour.
action: Simmer the brine, pour it over snugly packed vegetables, and let it cool to room temperature before chilling.
mechanism: Heat speeds the brine's diffusion into the vegetable while a quick cool keeps the texture crisp rather than cooked.
render_hint: Reference the actual vegetables and the brine ratio in this recipe.
source_note: interpreted from general quick-pickling technique

title: Salt watery vegetables first or the dish turns soggy
claim: Salting high-moisture vegetables pulls out water before they go into a slaw, salad, or saute, concentrating flavor and stopping dilution.
action: Toss the cut vegetables with salt, let them drain 15-30 minutes, then squeeze or pat dry before combining.
signal: A pool of liquid collecting in the bowl after the vegetables are dressed.
failure_mode: The finished slaw or salad goes watery and the dressing turns thin and bland within minutes.
mechanism: Salt draws water out of vegetable cells by osmosis, so the water leaves before it can dilute the dish.
render_hint: Name the specific watery vegetable in this recipe.
source_note: interpreted from general vegetable-salting technique

title: A splash of water cooks vegetables through evenly
claim: A little water steams firm vegetables to tenderness; once it cooks off, the same pan browns them, giving even texture without scorching.
action: Add a couple of tablespoons of water, cover briefly to steam, then uncover and let it evaporate so the vegetables brown.
mechanism: Water holds the pan at boiling temperature to cook the interior, then evaporates so the surface can climb hot enough to brown.
render_hint: Tie to the firm vegetable being cooked in this recipe.
source_note: interpreted from general sauteed-vegetable technique, aligned with ATK 100 Techniques #8

title: Steam dense vegetables before browning them
claim: Covering dense vegetables at the start traps steam to cook them through; uncovering then caramelizes the surface without leaving the inside raw.
action: Roast covered until just tender, then uncover and continue until the edges are deeply browned.
mechanism: Trapped steam conducts heat into the dense interior; removing the cover lets the surface dry and caramelize.
render_hint: Name the dense vegetable from this recipe.
source_note: interpreted from general steam-roasting technique, aligned with ATK 100 Techniques #9

title: Save pasta water before draining
claim: Starchy cooking water emulsifies fat and sauce into a glossy coating that clings to the pasta; without it the sauce slides off and looks oily.
action: Scoop out a cup of cooking water before draining, then add it a splash at a time while tossing pasta and sauce.
signal: Pasta and sauce refusing to come together, with a slick of oil separating out.
failure_mode: Sauce pools at the bottom of the bowl instead of coating the noodles, and the dish looks greasy.
mechanism: Dissolved starch acts as an emulsifier, binding fat and water into a sauce that coats the noodles.
render_hint: Reference the specific pasta shape and sauce in this recipe.
source_note: interpreted from general pasta-water technique, aligned with ATK 100 Techniques #10

title: Bright tomato sauce doesn't need hours
claim: A short, brisk cook keeps tomatoes fresh and fruity; long simmering trades that brightness for a flat, cooked-down flavor.
action: Cook the sauce hard and fast just until thickened, and finish with raw olive oil or fresh basil for lift.
mechanism: Tomatoes thicken as moisture evaporates; a quick reduction concentrates them while preserving volatile fresh-tomato aromas that long cooking drives off.
render_hint: Reference the tomato product and aromatics this recipe uses.
source_note: interpreted from general fresh tomato sauce technique

title: Cook the roux to the color the recipe specifies
claim: Cooking flour in fat both removes its raw taste and coats the granules so they disperse without lumping; how dark you take it sets both the flavor and the thickening power.
action: Whisk to a smooth paste and cook to the color the recipe calls for and no further, since a darker roux thickens less.
signal: A raw-flour smell or visible lumps mean it needs more cooking and whisking; an acrid smell or brown specks on the pan mean it's scorching.
failure_mode: Under-cooked roux leaves a raw, pasty taste and a soupy sauce; over-darkened roux loses thickening power and turns the dish gluey.

variants.note: Usually butter, cooked briefly over medium-low; for bechamel and cream sauces. Undercook it and the sauce won't set.
Often oil; cooked much longer to a deep brown for nutty flavor in gumbo and etouffee, with less thickening power.
Toast flour alone in the oven until browned, then whisk it with a little liquid before adding so it doesn't clump.

mechanism: Fat coats the starch granules so they separate and disperse smoothly; browning builds flavor but breaks down the starch that does the thickening.
render_hint: Reference how dark this recipe wants the roux and pick the matching variant.
source_note: interpreted from general roux technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #12

title: Soak rice noodles, don't hard-boil them
claim: Rice noodles overcook fast; a soak in hot rather than boiling water leaves them pliable but firm so they finish in the stir-fry without turning gummy.
action: Soak in hot water until just bendable but still firm, drain, and let them finish cooking in the sauce or stir-fry.
signal: Noodles already falling apart or sticking in a mass when drained.
failure_mode: Soft, gummy, clumped noodles before the dish is even assembled.
mechanism: Rice starch hydrates and softens quickly; gentler heat hydrates without gelatinizing the noodle into mush before the final toss.
render_hint: Reference the noodle width and how this recipe finishes them.
source_note: interpreted from general rice-noodle technique

title: Baking rice gives even, hands-off results
claim: The oven's surrounding heat cooks rice more evenly than a single burner, avoiding the scorched bottom and mushy top of an uneven flame.
action: Combine the rice with measured hot liquid, cover tightly, bake, and fluff with a fork at the end.
mechanism: Even, all-around oven heat removes the hot spot a burner creates under the pot, so the grains cook uniformly.
render_hint: Reference the rice type and liquid ratio in this recipe.
source_note: interpreted from general baked-rice technique

title: Build a pan sauce on the browned bits
claim: The browned residue left after searing a protein (the fond) is concentrated flavor; deglazing dissolves it into a fast, rich sauce in minutes.
action: Leave the fond in the pan, saute aromatics, deglaze with stock or wine while scraping, reduce, brighten with a little acid near the end, and whisk in cold butter off the heat.

variants.note: Build the sauce in a stainless skillet, not nonstick, so the flavorful fond sticks to the pan rather than the food.
Whisk in chilled butter off the heat, a piece at a time, for a glossy sauce that won't break.

mechanism: Fond is water-soluble browned flavor; liquid dissolves it, reduction concentrates it, and an off-heat butter emulsion enriches it without splitting.
render_hint: Reference the protein just cooked and the deglazing liquid this recipe specifies; note butter goes in off heat.
source_note: interpreted from general pan-sauce technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #15

title: Flip a thick steak often to avoid a gray band
claim: A thick steak browns best in an evenly heated, ripping-hot pan with frequent flipping; turning it every couple of minutes builds a crust while preventing a thick band of overcooked gray meat beneath it.
action: Dry and salt the steak, preheat the pan evenly, use generous oil, and flip about every 2 minutes, dropping the heat partway through, then rest before slicing.
signal: A thick gray ring forming under the crust, or a pale surface that means the pan wasn't hot enough.
failure_mode: An overcooked gray band beneath the crust, or weak browning from a too-cool or unevenly heated pan.

variants.note: Flip every ~2 minutes and drop from medium-high to medium-low partway so the outside browns without overcooking the center.
Cast iron sears hard but heats unevenly; preheat it in the oven for an even surface before searing.

mechanism: Frequent flipping keeps either face from overheating, so the interior cooks evenly while the surface still browns.
render_hint: This differs from delicate proteins: for steak, frequent flipping is correct, so do NOT tell the cook to leave it undisturbed.
source_note: interpreted from general steak-searing technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #16

title: Overworking ground meat makes tough burgers
claim: Overworking ground meat makes it dense and rubbery; gentle handling, and salting the outside rather than mixing salt in, keeps burgers tender and juicy.
action: Mix and shape with your hands just until it holds together, press a divot in each patty, season the exteriors, and cook flipping once without pressing down.
signal: A tacky, paste-like texture in the bowl, or patties that feel hard and compact.
failure_mode: Dense, rubbery, domed burgers, or dry ones if the meat is too lean or gets pressed during cooking.

variants.note: Salt the outsides of the formed patties; mixing salt into the meat dissolves proteins and toughens it.
Press a shallow divot in the center so the patty cooks flat instead of bulging into a ball.
85% lean beef or 93% lean poultry stays juicy; very lean grinds cook up dry and chalky.
Flip once and never press down, which squeezes out the juices.

mechanism: Working ground meat releases sticky soluble proteins that bind it into a dense mass; salt mixed in does the same, so both are minimized.
render_hint: Reference the specific ground meat in this recipe; pull in only the variants the recipe's steps touch.
source_note: interpreted from general ground-meat handling technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #17

title: Let flaky fish form a crust, then flip with two spatulas
claim: Flaky fish sticks and tears if it's wet or moved too soon; a dry surface, a smoking-hot pan, and two thin spatulas for turning keep delicate fillets golden and intact.
action: Salt and pat the fillets dry, cook in a hot nonstick pan until the first side is golden and releases, then turn once using two thin spatulas.
signal: The fillet resisting and flaking when you slide a spatula under it means the crust hasn't set; tearing means it was moved too soon.
failure_mode: Fish sticks to the pan and breaks apart, or steams pale and gray instead of browning.

variants.note: Cut along the natural center seam and cook the thicker and thinner halves separately so each browns evenly.
Start over high heat then lower it to brown the outside without overcooking the center; a pinch of sugar in the salt rub speeds browning.

mechanism: A dry surface lets the pan brown rather than steam the fish, and a set crust releases cleanly; two spatulas support the fragile fillet through the flip.
render_hint: Name the fish and whether this recipe cooks it skin-on; pick the thin/thick variant to match.
source_note: interpreted from general fish-sauteing technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #18

title: Dry scallops and don't crowd them, or they steam
claim: Scallops carry a lot of surface moisture; unless they're dried well and seared in a hot, uncrowded nonstick pan, they steam in their own liquid and turn rubbery before a crust forms.
action: Remove the side tendon, blot the scallops very dry, sear in batches in a smoking-hot pan without moving them, then baste with butter as you finish the second side.
signal: Liquid pooling and a dull, wet surface instead of an active sear means the scallops are steaming.
failure_mode: Pale, rubbery, overcooked scallops with no golden crust.

variants.note: Choose 'dry' (untreated) scallops; 'wet' ones are treated with STPP, which adds moisture that blocks browning and brings off-flavors.
After searing the first side, add butter and spoon it over to deepen browning and flavor without burning.

mechanism: Surface water must evaporate before browning starts; thorough drying plus high, uncrowded heat get the surface there before the interior overcooks.
render_hint: Reference the scallop size and the crust color this recipe wants.
source_note: interpreted from general scallop-searing technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #19

title: Crowding a stir-fry steams it; prep ahead and work in batches
claim: A home burner can't keep a crowded pan hot, so a piled-in stir-fry steams; bite-size pieces, small batches, and everything prepped in advance keep the heat up and the food browning.
action: Cut everything small and mix the sauce before heating the pan, then cook the protein in batches over high heat, add ingredients in stages, and add aromatics near the end.
signal: The pan going quiet and filling with liquid once food is added means it's overcrowded and steaming.
failure_mode: Soggy vegetables and gray, steamed meat that never browns.

variants.note: Stir-fries cook in a flash, so everything must be cut and the sauce mixed before the pan goes on the heat.
Despite the name, leave the food alone in spurts so it can brown and caramelize rather than just steam.
An exception to high heat: start shrimp over medium-low so they don't toughen.

mechanism: Browning needs sustained high surface heat; small batches and a flat pan keep the temperature up so food sears instead of releasing water and steaming.
render_hint: Reference the specific proteins and vegetables, and remind the cook to prep everything before the pan heats.
source_note: interpreted from general stir-fry technique, cross-checked against ATK 100 Techniques #20
